paras: The lynchings at Dady, Florida, took place on July 30, 1910, when a mob of white men took two Black men accused of murdering a white schoolgirl from the Holmes County sheriff and hanged and shot them on a road between Dady and Bonifay. Later dispatches reported a manhunt and further killings, putting the toll anywhere from one to six; the Pensacola Journal said a reported fourth killing had not happened. Some Black newspapers carried the story as short wire items.

Bessie Morrison, described as 12 or 14 years old, was the daughter of Mrs. Mary Morrison, who lived near Dady in the western end of Holmes County. She left alone for school on Friday, July 29, and did not come home; a search party found her body in a pool of water in a swamp near her home. Two Black men who worked at a turpentine camp were arrested at Dady, and the papers said they confessed to assaulting and killing her.

As the sheriff and two assistants took the prisoners toward the county jail, residents followed, overtook the sheriff "in a lonely road," overpowered him and took the men to the nearest tree, where ropes had already been prepared. The Ocala Evening Star's Bonifay dispatch said the two were "pleading vainly for their lives" as fifty to seventy-five white men hanged them and fired bullets into their bodies. According to the sheriff, the mob could not be controlled, and "white blood would be spilled" had he refused to give up the prisoners.

On August 1 the Associated Press reported from Pensacola that telephone wires had been cut, farmers were joining posses, and Black residents were "fleeing for their lives." The same wire said an unnamed Black man who had lent a good-luck amulet to one of the accused was captured, hanged and shot, the fourth lynched for the crime. The Montgomery Advertiser said instead that he had lent a mule and was caught in a swamp and hanged. On August 2 posses were still searching the woods, and several Black men were reported fired on, with no more deaths.

The Pensacola Journal reported from DeFuniak Springs on August 2 that "careful investigation" showed the rumored killing of the fourth man was untrue; no evidence tied him to the crime and the posse released him. A sheriff, printed as Kell and as Bell, left Bonifay with a posse to stop further trouble. No report of an inquest, an arrest of any mob member or a grand jury inquiry appears in the coverage.

Southern papers framed the hanging as revenge: the Ocala Evening Star headed its report "An Awful Crime Avenged," and the version reprinted in South Carolina called the accused "negro fiends" whose crime was "quickly avenged by citizens." The New-York Tribune put the AP count under the headline "Whites Take Good Measure for Florida Murder," and a North Dakota weekly headed the De Funiak Springs item "Another Bad Negro Gone."

Outside Florida the toll grew with time: Montgomery reported three, the AP four, and an Ohio weekly a "reign of terror" with four lynched after the first two. The Florida papers closest to the scene moved the other way, with the Ocala Evening Star reporting only one man hanged and the Pensacola Journal denying the fourth killing.

The Black press coverage found consists of wire items, with no editorial comment. The Advocate printed the highest count, "Six Negroes Are Lynched in Florida," saying a reign of terror existed and "wholesale killing of Negroes" was planned. The Colorado Statesman repeated the two-man item, the Cleveland Gazette the "reign of terror" dispatch, and the Boley Progress a line that four were lynched for the killing of "Besie Morris."

Most first reports said two men were hanged on July 30, but the Montgomery Advertiser said three, and the Ocala Evening Star later said the mob gave one of the two back to the officers, who jailed him. The fourth killing reported on August 1 by the AP and the Montgomery Advertiser was denied by the Pensacola Journal after local inquiry, and the Advocate's count of six appears in no other report; none of the reports names any of the dead.

reader.title: Lynchings at Dady, Florida
bases: A mob of fifty to seventy-five white men overtook the sheriff on the road, took two accused Black men from him and hanged and shot them (A1, A18, A11).

Two Black men accused of the assault and murder of a white girl were taken from the sheriff by fifty to seventy-five men and hanged and shot (A1, A18); the number killed is disputed, from one (A8) to six (A17), but every report has at least one man hanged by the mob.

Several separately written dispatches from Bonifay, Pensacola and De Funiak Springs agree that a mob took accused men from the sheriff and hanged them (A1, A4, A11, A8), though the number killed is contested (A8, A15, A17).

accounts.label: Bonifay first report
accounts.gist: Two men who confessed were taken from the sheriff on a lonely road by fifty to seventy-five men, hanged, and their bodies shot; the sheriff said resistance would have spilled white blood.

accounts.label: Montgomery Advertiser Pensacola specials
accounts.gist: Three men were lynched on the night of July 30, and a fourth, said to have lent a mule to one of them, was caught in a swamp and hanged on Aug. 1.

accounts.label: AP Pensacola wire
accounts.gist: An unnamed man who had lent a good-luck amulet to one of the accused was hanged and shot on Aug. 1, the fourth lynched, while wires were cut and Black residents fled.

accounts.label: Ocala Evening Star correction
accounts.gist: Only one man was hanged; the mob decided the other should not be held and gave him back to the officers, who jailed him.

accounts.label: Pensacola Journal correction
accounts.gist: The reported killing of a fourth man was untrue; no evidence tied him to the crime and the posse released him.

accounts.label: Advocate (Bonifay dispatch)
accounts.gist: Two more men were lynched on Aug. 2, making six, and a reign of terror with wholesale killing was expected.

framing.detail: Headlines such as 'An Awful Crime Avenged' and 'The Brutal Murder of a Little Girl Is Quickly Avenged by Citizens' called the accused 'negro fiends' and the lynching vengeance.
The New-York Tribune headed the AP count 'Whites Take Good Measure for Florida Murder'.
Northern and Midwestern papers ran one-line wire items on two men lynched after confessing.
Later dispatches described a 'reign of terror' and whites seeking 'wholesale lynching' without comment.
The Advocate, Colorado Statesman, Cleveland Gazette and Boley Progress ran wire items, the Advocate under 'Six Negroes Are Lynched in Florida', with no editorial comment found.

conflicts.note: The two-man hanging on July 30 is the most widely reported; the Aug. 1 'fourth' killing was denied by the local Pensacola Journal after investigation (A15), and the Advocate's six stands alone.
Pensacola Journal says he was not killed and was released (A15).
Probably one name garbled in transmission.
